nameStory: Mountain woodsorrel gets its name from its natural habitat in mountainous and elevated areas, where it thrives in cool, shaded forests. The 'sorrel' part comes from the sour taste of its leaves, which contain oxalic acid - the same compound that gives rhubarb its tang. Early settlers and Indigenous peoples would nibble the leaves as a vitamin C-rich snack, calling various sour-leaved plants 'sorrels.'
description: Mountain woodsorrel is a delicate woodland perennial that looks like a tiny shamrock growing close to the ground. This charming little plant reaches only 2-6 inches tall, with three heart-shaped leaflets that fold up like umbrellas when touched or at night. Its white flowers have delicate pink veins and five petals, appearing singly on thin stems above the clover-like leaves. The entire plant has a soft, almost fragile appearance that perfectly suits its shady forest home.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets that fold upward when touched, disturbed, or in bright light - like tiny green umbrellas closing up. The leaflets are soft and tender with a distinctly sour taste when chewed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five white petals with delicate pink or purple veins running through them, appearing singly on thin, curved stems. Flowers are about half an inch across and have a sweet, subtle fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial that forms small colonies, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall. Leaves and flowers emerge directly from creeping underground stems called rhizomes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, pointed capsules that explosively pop open when ripe, shooting tiny brown seeds several feet away with an audible 'tick' sound when touched.

habitat: Mountain woodsorrel thrives in cool, moist, shaded areas of northern and mountain forests throughout New England. Look for it under conifers and mixed hardwood forests, especially in areas with rich, acidic soil and good leaf litter. It's most common at higher elevations and in the cooler microclimates of ravines, north-facing slopes, and deep woods where the canopy keeps conditions consistently cool and moist.

seasonality.spring: Fresh three-parted leaves emerge in early spring, followed by the first white flowers in late April through May. This is the best time to see the plant at its most vigorous.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering sporadically through summer in cool locations. Leaves remain green and respond dramatically to touch by folding upward within seconds.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and begin their explosive dispersal. Leaves may persist into early fall in protected locations before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Mountain woodsorrel's leaves can fold up and 'sleep' in just 15 seconds when touched, and they also do this automatically every evening at dusk, then reopen in the morning - giving the plant a daily bedtime routine just like animals!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the other white-flowered woodsorrel, Oxalis acetosella, but that European species is rare in New England. The yellow woodsorrels have similar leaves but bright yellow flowers instead of white. Remember: white flowers usually mean mountain woodsorrel in New England forests.
contextualKnowledge: Mountain woodsorrel is sometimes called 'wood shamrock' and gets mistakenly picked for St. Patrick's Day decorations, but true shamrock refers to clover species. Some botanists consider our mountain woodsorrel to be the same species as European Oxalis acetosella, just a North American variety, which explains why identification guides sometimes conflict on the scientific name.
compareHints: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones. Unlike the upright yellow woodsorrel that grows in sunny, disturbed areas, mountain woodsorrel strictly prefers deep shade and undisturbed forest floors. The explosive seed pods are common to most woodsorrels, but the combination of white flowers and forest habitat makes mountain woodsorrel distinctive among New England's woodsorrels.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
